title: Why I Sold My Individual Bonds and Moved Everything Into 1 Bond ETF
detail:
Why I Sold My Individual Bonds and Moved Everything Into 1 Bond ETF
Todd Shriber, The Motley Fool

NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors are often taught the virtues of diversification when it comes to stocks. It's an excellent idea to build equity portfolios comprised of numerous stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), preferably across a variety of industries and sectors, so that when one asset sneezes, the whole portfolio doesn't catch a cold.

The wisdom of diversification is also applicable to bonds. For investors who are new to the fixed-income arena, note that while bonds won't match stocks for long-term upside, they are useful for generating income, diversifying portfolios, and potentially limiting volatility when the stock market is turbulent.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF is a better idea than owning individual bonds. Image source: Getty Images.

However, some of those perks can be mitigated when buying individual bonds. Select the wrong issue, and an investor can limit their income potential or bite off a bond that's highly correlated with stocks, muting their portfolio's diversification.

In other words, as is the case with owning just one stock, it's risky to own a single bond. The Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF (NASDAQ: BND), the largest fixed-income ETF, solves that problem.

I let BND do the bond work for me

These days, investors are hearing plenty about interest rates. That situation is amplified by the fact that the Federal Reserve recently raised rates and is expected to do so once more before the end of 2026 as part of its effort to quash inflation.

Rising rates are also a reminder that when investing in bonds and ETFs, such as the Vanguard fund, for that matter, there are two forms of risk that market participants must consider: rate risk and credit risk. Both of those potential headwinds highlight the advantages of considering a broad-based ETF such as this Vanguard fund.

For example, 30-year Treasuries don't carry much credit risk; not yet anyway. But if rates rise by 1%, those funds can subject investors to deep double-digit losses, which is to say a bond many investors view as risk-free is far from that.

Further underscoring the perks of an ETF, such as the Vanguard fund, is its low credit risk. There is a slew of high-yield corporate bonds, also known as "junk" bonds, on the market sporting yields well in excess of those of the S&P 500, long-dated Treasuries, and even many high-dividend stocks. But pick the wrong junk bond, and an investor could endure credit downgrades, or worse, defaults, and see the value of their investment greatly diminished.

title: Why Arm Holdings Stock Was Falling Today

Why Arm Holdings Stock Was Falling Today

Shares of Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) were falling today amid a broader sell-off in tech and chip stocks after the September Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in hotter than expected.

That was enough to send tech stocks swooning as it makes it more likely that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting later this month.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Arm is especially sensitive to interest rates because most of the stock's value comes from earnings that are several years into the future, as investors are betting on strong profits from its new AGI CPU, which has yet to go on sale.

As of 3:13 p.m ET, Arm stock was down 6.7% on the news.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

What happened with the CPI

The Consumer Price Index is one of the most important data points in determining the Fed's action on interest rates, and faster-than-expected inflation is more likely to trigger a rate hike to help slow the economy down and reel in inflation.

The CPI rose 3.7% on an annual basis last month, ahead of expectations at 3.6%, while core CPI, which strips out the volatile food and energy categories, was up 2.6%, compared to expectations of 2.5% growth.

Energy prices continue to surge due to the war in Iran, up 5.2% from August, and gasoline was up 9.1%.

What it means for Arm

Inflation doesn't directly impact Arm. While the company's chip designs are found in smartphones and an array of other consumer devices, the stock is down because of valuation-related adjustments. As interest rates go up, the discount rate in the discounted cash flow also goes up, and that makes earnings in the future less valuable than they were.

Investors should expect Arm stock to continue moving up and down according to interest rate expectations.

With the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) near all-time highs, it may be surprising to learn that more than 25% of the index's stocks are down 40% or more from their highs, as of Oct. 8, 2026. That's a shocking number, but it also gives investors the opportunity to go bargain hunting.

Let's look at four stocks to scoop up today.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Netflix

Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) shares have tumbled as the streaming giant's growth has slowed. However, there is still a lot to like about the stock.

The company tends to be recession-resistant as a cheap form of entertainment, and it is making a big push with advertising, which should become its biggest growth driver in the coming years. It also has the potential to continue adding subscribers, and it has shown pricing power with its ad-free tier.

Trading at a forward P/E of around 18.5 times 2027 analyst estimates, it's a solid stock to scoop up at current levels.

2. Oracle

Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) has become one of the biggest battlegrounds among artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. The company is seeing major growth in its cloud computing infrastructure business, and it has one of the largest backlogs in the space, at $664 billion as of the end of Q2.

However, this is a company already carrying considerable debt and burning cash. Meanwhile, Oracle has been trying to get creative with its financing, including setting up a separate entity to buy chips and then lease them out. This adds risk, but cloud computing economics are strong and tend to have relatively quick paybacks of two to three years, or even sooner.

Ultimately, Oracle's leverage and beaten-down stock price could give it more upside in the space if the cloud model proves to work, and many great companies are betting it will.

3. ServiceNow

ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW) is a stock that has gotten caught up in the software-as-a-service (SaaS) sell-off in 2026 despite being one of the best-positioned software companies for the age of agentic AI. Its platform is one of the most deeply embedded of any software company, with its solution used to run organizations' entire software stacks and its configuration management database (CMDB) linking the underlying relationships between hardware, software, cloud services, and business processes.

The company has leaned into AI and cybersecurity to drive growth, and it's looking to become an important agentic AI orchestration platform with its AI Control Tower solution. With the proliferation of AI agents from a plethora of vendors, monitoring, managing, and securing them within an organization will become vital, and ServiceNow appears to be the most likely leader in this space. With a forward price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 7.5 times based on 2027 analyst estimates, the stock is attractively valued given its opportunity.

Why SandiskStock Keeps Going Down

This is starting to look serious. Tic-tac-toe, three days in a row, Sandisk (Nasdaq: SNDK) stock has gone nowhere but down. Adding Wednesday's 4.6% decline (as of 2:35 p.m. ET) to similar declines Monday and Tuesday, shares of Sandisk -- one of the world's biggest makers of computer memory chips -- are now down 11% for the week, and approaching a 20% loss for the month.

Don't say you were not warned.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

What's dogging Sandisk stock this week

As far back as Monday -- my, how time flies! -- I warned that this downturn had the potential to turn into a rout, as investors worried over news that Chinese DRAM company CXMT -- which makes DRAM memory chips -- was closing its technology gap with Western memory chipmakers.

CXMT bragged on Monday that it is making "key progress" on "4F square" technology to increase DRAM storage density. It further promised to introduce products targeting the market for high bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI data centers before the end of this year.

The last time something like this happened, Sandisk stock got cut nearly in half.

What's next for Sandisk stock

And yet, several things are worth remembering for investors spooked by the Sandisk sell-off. First and foremost: CXMT makes DRAM memory, but Sandisk doesn't. Instead, Sandisk makes NAND, a related technology that can be used similarly to HBM in a form that Sandisk calls "high bandwidth flash".

But they're not directly comparable, and CXMT is not a direct competitor to Sandisk.

It may not even be much of a competitor to Micron. In a note on StreetInsider.com today, Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein points out that while CXMT promised to "introduce" its 4F square product in 2026, it's probably years away from producing the chips at scale. He also doubts the CXMT product is comparable to HBM chips that Micron builds today, or to Sandisk's HBF. Most likely, it's an ordinary DRAM chip not suitable for AI data centers at all.

TL;DR Sandisk investors are panicking over this. They shouldn't.

The Stock Market Just Flashed a Warning Signal That’s Been Right 83% of the Time Since 1960. Here’s My Plan.
Matt DiLallo, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 12:50 PM CDT 5 min read
NVDA

Investors are borrowing heavily against their portfolios to boost their returns. Over the past year, margin debt has increased by 49%. That's a bad omen. According to Fundstrat Global Advisors, whenever margin debt has grown more than 45% year-over-year since 1960, the market has declined five out of six times (83%). That's a signal worth watching.

However, while the market is flashing a warning sign, I'm not panicking. Instead, I'm making an action plan to position my portfolio to better weather a potential market storm and capitalize on opportunities that may arise.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

The warning signs abound

Fundstrat found that surging margin debt has historically preceded a market decline. The firm found that the median performance of the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) following a 40% surge in margin debt is a 4.2% decline over the next 12 months. They also found that the more margin debt rises, the worse the market's subsequent returns over the next 12-month period. One factor is that investors need to quickly unwind their margin debt when the market starts declining, which exacerbates selling.

This signal isn't the only one flashing these days. The CAPE ratio recently hit its second-highest reading on record. Meanwhile, stocks have historically fallen after the Federal Reserve begins a rate-hike cycle (it recently raised rates for the first time in three years).

My action plan

While these warning signs aren't making me bearish, they are making me more cautious. That's why I've been building cash by selling some lower-conviction holdings and being more selective in new investments. I'm focusing on less volatile options, such as high-quality dividend-paying stocks, especially those with long track records of dividend growth.

Data from Ned Davis Research and Hartford Funds shows that dividend growers deliver the highest total returns with the lowest volatility compared to companies that don't grow their dividends and those that don't pay dividends. My favorite way to invest in the highest-quality dividend growth stocks is through the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEMKT:SCHD). The fund holds 100 top dividend stocks screened by several quality characteristics, including five-year dividend growth rate, current yield, and financial strength. The ETF currently offers a 3% yield (based on its trailing 12-month distribution rate) and holds companies that have increased their dividends at an average annual rate of more than 9% over the past five years.

Netflix is slashing 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, The Wall Street Journal scooped on Wednesday. It's the streaming giant's largest layoff since 2022, when it shed roughly 450 jobs after posting its first subscriber loss in a decade.

"Our mission—to entertain the world—is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos said in an email obtained by WSJ on Wednesday morning. The cuts will hit legal, tech, product, and HR teams.

The memo also insisted the business is "strong and growing" and on track to hit its full-year forecast. Wall Street isn't so sure. The key problem, here, is attention, with lots of video, social and streaming services competing for it: YouTube grabbed a record 14.2% of US TV viewing in July, per Nielsen data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence, while Netflix's share slid to a multiyear low of 7.8%.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

Analysts have noticed. Wells Fargo downgraded the stock to underweight in September, warning that viewing hours for Netflix's top 100 originals could drop 21% year over year in the back half of this year. HSBC followed with its own downgrade days later.

Netflix also lost its biggest swing at scale. It walked away from its Warner Bros. Discovery bid in February, pocketing a $2.8 billion breakup fee as Paramount Skydance took the prize. A Paramount-Warner combo is one more rival fighting for the same eyeballs.

Netflix stock is down over 23% since January 1. The S&P 500 is up over 12%. The company will report earnings next week, so clearly the pruning is with an eye toward welcoming analysts into the garden.
